item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Richie Palacios dropped a blooper into shallow right in the ninth inning to score Junior Caminero and give the Tampa Bay Rays a 2-1 victory over the Boston Red Sox on Saturday.
Tampa Bay, which has three walk-off wins on its current homestand, lowered its magic number to clinch the AL East to five games. The second-place Yankees are in Arizona on Saturday night.
Prior to Palacios’ single, the Rays were 0 for 17 with runners in scoring position over the first two games of the series. The postseason-bound Rays, who’ve won seven of their last eight, capitalized on two fortuitous bounces in the ninth.
First, Caminero’s foul popup bounced off the Tropicana Field catwalk and out of the reach of third baseman Caleb Durbin. Caminero then lined the next pitch from Garrett Whitlock (7-2) into left. Three batters later, after Chandler Simpson singled, Connor Wong’s passed ball moved Caminero to third.
Bidding to clinch a wild-card berth, the Red Sox squandered a prime opportunity in the top of the ninth.
Facing closer Bryan Baker (4-2) in a tie game, Boston got a double from Caleb Durbin and a triple from Jarren Duran. However, Nick Fortes threw out Durbin stealing third before Duran’s triple, and Caminero made a stellar play at third base to retire Isiah Kiner-Falefa, stranding Duran.
Boston also wasted a phenomenal effort from starter Brayan Bello, who matched a career high with 11 strikeouts. In eight innings, he allowed five hits, one run and no walks. Red Sox closer Aroldis Chapman (lat tightness) was unavailable.
The Red Sox took a 1-0 lead with doubles from Durbin and Roman Anthony in the third inning. Trevor Story extended his hitting streak to 10 games with a sixth-inning single.
Jonathan Aranda tied it with an opposite-field solo homer on the first pitch of the Rays’ fourth.
The Rays are an MLB-best 25-14 in one-run games.
Boston could have clinched a playoff berth with a win combined with a loss by either the Rangers or Astros. Both of those teams were seven games behind the Red Sox with eight games remaining entering Saturday.
UP NEXT
Right-hander Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80 ERA) gets the nod for the Rays on Sunday in the series finale. Boston had not announced a starter.

item.content:encoded:
The Tampa Bay Rays (94-60) defeated the Boston Red Sox (84-71) 2-1 on Saturday evening at Tropicana Field. With the win, the Rays have evened the three-game series as they continue a push to try to win the American League East crown.
The Red Sox got on the board in the third inning thanks to a RBI double from Roman Anthony. In the bottom of the fourth, Jonathan Aranda hit a solo homer to tie the game 1-1. That would remain the score until the bottom of the ninth inning.
Junior Caminero led off the bottom of the ninth with a single to left, before Jonny DeLuca popped out. Chandler Simpson then hit a single to put runners on first and second, before those runners both advanced thanks to a passed ball from Red Sox catcher Connor Wong. Victor Mesa Jr then struck out before Richie Palacios came to the plate. With runners on second and third and two outs, Palacios singled on a shallow fly ball to right field that fell in and allowed the Rays to leave Tropicana Field as walk-off winners.
Freddy Peralta got the start and allowed just one earned run on four hits in five and two-third innings of work in which he struck out six and walked two. Bryan Baker (4-2, 1.49) picked up the win out of the bullpen after working a scoreless top of the ninth inning.
The Rays will now try to win the series against the Red Sox when they meet in the finale on Sunday afternoon. Griffin Jax (7-10, 3.80) is scheduled to start for the Rays and face Patrick Sandoval (1-6, 4.99) for the Red Sox. First pitch on Sunday is scheduled for 1:40 PM - pregame coverage begins at 1:00 PM on 95.7 WDAE.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — Brayan Bello, a pitcher who lost his spot in the rotation earlier in this season, did his best to pitch the Red Sox into the postseason on Saturday afternoon, allowing one run over eight innings against the Rays.
But it was not enough.
The Rays walked-off the Sox in the ninth inning with a 2-1 victory before a crowd of 27,402 at Tropicana Field as Richie Palacios had a two-out run-scoring single.
Bello gave up only five hits and struck out 11 — matching his career high — without a walk.
The loss left the Red Sox with a magic number of two.
In a tense game between two teams who could well meet in October, the Sox missed numerous chances to score. They were for 1 for 11 with runners in scoring position and left eight runners on base.
They left a runner on second in the eighth inning and another on third in the ninth.
Facing Garrett Whitlock (7-2) in the ninth inning, Junior Caminero led off with a single — after his potentially playable foul popup struck a catwalk and was ruled a dead ball.
Chandler Simpson singled with one out. A passed ball by Connor Wong moved the runners up. Palacios then won the game with a soft single to shallow right field.
The early innings were a duel between Bello and Rays starter Freddy Peralta.
Peralta retired the first six Red Sox in order, four by swinging strikeout. Caleb Durbin led off the third inning with a double to left field. Jarren Duran sacrificed Durbin to third before Roman Anthony delivered an RBI double to center field.
The Rays tied the game when Jonathan Aranda led off the bottom of the fourth inning with a home run to left field when Bello left a first-pitch fastball over the plate.
Peralta gave up four hits and walked two over 5⅔ innings and 97 pitches but allowed only the one run. The Sox were 1 for 7 with runners in scoring position against him.
Bello had only 68 pitches through six innings. Liam Hicks and Simpson singled on his first two pitches of the seventh inning. With Jonny DeLuca running for Hicks, the runners moved up when Victor Mesa Jr. grounded to second.
With the infield in, Palacios grounded to shortstop. Trevor Story snapped the ball up and fired to the plate to get DeLuca. Bello then struck out Cedric Mullins with a 96.8-mile-per-hour fastball.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox could not have asked much more from Brayan Bello on Saturday. Unfortunately for Boston, nearly everything around him went wrong at the worst possible moments.
Bello delivered eight outstanding innings, but the Red Sox squandered several scoring opportunities before the Tampa Bay Rays walked off with a 2-1 victory at Tropicana Field. Richie Palacios ended the game with a two-out single off Garrett Whitlock, bringing Junior Caminero home from third base. The loss dropped Boston to 84-71 and evened the three-game series at one victory apiece.
Here are four takeaways from Saturday’s game:
Bello Brilliant In Tough-Luck Start
Bello did everything necessary to earn a victory. The right-hander allowed only one earned run on five hits over eight innings. He did not issue a walk, struck out 11 and threw 65 of his 93 pitches for strikes.
FINAL: Rays 2, #RedSox 1
— Red Sox (@RedSox) September 19, 2026
Bello retired the first three batters he faced and struck out seven through his first five innings. Tampa Bay’s only run against him came when Jonathan Aranda opened the fourth inning with a 361-foot home run.
The Rays threatened again in the seventh after singles from Lathan Hicks and Chandler Simpson placed two runners aboard with nobody out. Bello escaped without allowing a run, getting Víctor Mesa Jr. on a groundout, Palacios on a fielder’s choice at the plate and Cedric Mullins on a strikeout.
Bello finished the eighth by retiring Tampa Bay in order. He set down 17 of the final 20 hitters he faced and ended the afternoon with a season-high 11 strikeouts.
Boston Offense Wastes Its Chances
The Red Sox collected eight hits but finished only 1-for-11 with runners in scoring position and stranded eight runners. Boston scored its only run in the third inning. Caleb Durbin opened the frame with a double, advanced to third on Jarren Duran’s sacrifice bunt and scored when Roman Anthony doubled to center field.
That was all the Red Sox produced against Freddy Peralta and four Tampa Bay relievers.
Boston placed two runners aboard in both the fourth and sixth innings without scoring. Adley Rutschman doubled with one out in the eighth, but Wilyer Abreu struck out and Nick Sogard lined out to end the threat.
The most frustrating missed opportunity arrived in the ninth.
Durbin doubled with one out but was caught trying to steal third. Duran then tripled to center field, a hit that almost certainly would have scored Durbin had he remained at second. Isiah Kiner-Falefa grounded out to strand Duran and keep the game tied.
Ninth Inning Unravels On Whitlock
Whitlock entered for the bottom of the ninth after Bello’s terrific afternoon and immediately surrendered a single to Caminero. Whitlock retired Jonny DeLuca before Simpson added another single. A passed ball charged to Connor Wong moved both runners into scoring position, although Whitlock responded by striking out Mesa for the second out.
He could not escape the inning.
Palacios lined a 2-2 sinker into right field, allowing Caminero to score the winning run. The run was unearned because of Wong’s passed ball, but Whitlock took the loss after surrendering three hits in two-thirds of an inning.
MORE: How the Red Sox Can Clinch a Playoff Spot on Saturday
Series Finale Takes On Added Importance
Boston entered Saturday with a chance to take another significant step toward securing its postseason spot after winning Friday’s series opener. Instead, the Red Sox will need to regroup quickly following one of their most frustrating losses of the season.
The defeat dropped Boston to 84-71 and left the Red Sox 10 1/2 games behind the first-place Rays in the American League East. More importantly, it prevented Boston from building additional momentum in the wild-card race.
The Red Sox and Rays will decide the series Sunday at Tropicana Field. First pitch is scheduled for 3:10 p.m. ET.

item.content:encoded:
ST. PETERSBURG, Fla. — The Tampa Bay Rays have been the best team in the American League for much of this season, particularly at Tropicana Field.
But with one All-Star on the injured list and two others unavailable, the Red Sox came away with a 4-2 victory before a crowd of 23,342 as Roman Anthony drove in three runs.
Now the magic number to clinch a playoff spot is down to two.
Ranger Suarez (8-4) and three relievers walked nine but held the Rays to five hits. Tampa Bay was hitless in 13 at-bats with runners in scoring position and left 12 men on base.
It was an impressive victory for the Sox, considering the 93-60 Rays are close to clinching the best record in the league and home-field advantage through, at least, the American League Championship Series.
The Sox were without Ceddanne Rafaela, who isn’t expected to come off the injured list until next week. Aroldis Chapman (lat strain) and Willson Contreras (bruised right hand) were not available.
With Garrett Whitlock left in the bullpen after pitching Thursday night, the Sox used lefthander Erik Miller to get the final three outs for his first save with the team.
Miller walked two and threw three wild pitches in a wild ninth inning, giving up a run before finally getting Chandler Simpson to ground to second for the final out.
Miller had allowed five runs over 5⅓ innings and put 10 men on base in his previous six appearances.
The Sox didn’t arrive at the team hotel until close to 5 a.m. after beating the Rangers in Texas on Thursday night. The Rays had a day game at home that ended 13 hours earlier. But the Sox had more energy early on.
Anthony blasted the third pitch of the game from Ian Seymour 438 feet to center field for his fifth home run.
Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the second inning with singles. Isiah Kiner-Falefa dropped a bunt to advance the runners before Nate Eaton worked a walk to load the bases.
After Connor Wong struck out, Anthony worked the count full and lined a hard single to right field to drive in two more runs. The three RBIs matched his career high.
Jahmai Jones homered leading off the third inning, a 414-foot shot to left field.
Suarez did not handle the run support very well. He walked a hitter in each of the first four innings and threw 69 pitches. But the Rays scored only one run.
Yandy Diaz walked leading off the bottom of the first, advanced to third on a double by Jonathan Aranda, and scored on Junior Caminero’s groundout.
Suarez was done after 5⅔ innings and 98 pitches, leaving the game with a runner at second. Wyatt Olds walked Liam Hicks and Victor Mesa Jr. on 12 pitches to load the bases.
He fell behind Jake Fraley 3 and 1, then came back to strike him out swinging through a fastball at the top of the strike zone. Olds threw up his hands after finally ending the inning. It wasn’t an elegant outing, but it was ultimately an effective one.
Greg Weissert worked around a two-out double by Caminero in the seventh inning to keep the lead at three runs, then came back for a 1-2-3 eighth.

item.content:encoded:
Back in late June when the Red Sox sunk to their lowest depths, the idea that the club might still have a shot at reaching the postseason would have seemed hopelessly optimistic.
Yet, here they are with a little over a week left to play in the regular season, and the Red Sox have all but punched their ticket to the playoffs.
With their 4-2 win over the Tampa Bay Rays in Friday’s series opener, the Red Sox can now clinch a playoff spot as soon as Saturday. The club’s magic number, which stood at three entering the night, will drop to either one or two depending on the outcome of Friday’s late game between the Rangers and Blue Jays.
A Rangers win would mean the Red Sox could clinch with a win on Saturday, while a Blue Jays win would necessitate a win and a Blue Jays loss.
Following a string of poor offensive performances, Friday got off to a much stronger start at the plate. Roman Anthony put the Red Sox in front with a solo home run to lead off the game, and after the Rays tied it up in the bottom half of the first, Anthony delivered again in the second with a go-ahead two-run single with the bases loaded off Rays starter Ian Seymour, an alumnus of St. John’s High School in Shrewsbury.
Anthony finished 2 for 4 with three RBI, and the Red Sox never looked back.
“Taking that first one is big,” Anthony told NESN’s Jahmai Webster postgame. “Any win you can get against a team like that it’s a great win, so it’s a great day.”
Anthony’s first-inning blast was smoked. Measured at 107.7 mph off the bat and traveling 438 feet, the solo home run to right field narrowly missed landing in Tropicana Field’s ray tank.
His two-run single in the second inning was hit even harder, coming off the bat at 108.7 mph. Anthony came through after Trevor Story and Caleb Durbin led off the inning with singles, Isiah Kiner-Falefa moved them into scoring position with a sacrifice bunt and Nate Eaton walked to load the bases.
It was doubly encouraging given Anthony’s recent struggles at the plate. After a hot start coming off the injured list, the outfielder came into Friday batting just .137 with one extra base hit over his past 12 games.
“I’ve been grinding, but that’s the beauty of this team,” Anthony said. “You’re never down and you’re never out.”
Jahmai Jones capped off the early offense with a solo shot to lead off the top of the third.
Tampa Bay scored its early run in the first after Yandy Diaz drew a leadoff walk, advanced to third on a Jonathan Aranda double and scored on a Junior Caminero groundout. But that was all the damage the Rays could do against Ranger Suarez, who allowed one run over 5 2/3 innings while falling one out short of his third consecutive quality start.
Suarez was uncharacteristically wild, walking five batters, but he limited the damage by allowing just three hits while striking out five.
The walks almost cost the Red Sox in the sixth inning.
Still leading by three, Suarez issued his fifth and final walk to lead off the sixth before recording two quick outs to finish his outing. But Wyatt Olds came on and immediately walked the first two men he faced, loading the bases and bringing the go-ahead run to the plate.
A brief mound visit followed, and Olds dug deep and struck out pinch hitter Jake Fraley to escape the inning unscathed.
“It was a weird game all the way around, we walked nine in total, Ranger walked five but still almost completed six innings and he was very competitive with men on base,” Red Sox interim manager Chad Tracy told reporters in St. Petersburg. “He lost some counts and behind more counts today, but he was able to make really good pitches with people on base.”
Walks put the Red Sox in one more jam in the bottom of the ninth inning.
With Aroldis Chapman unavailable with a lat issue and Garrett Whitlock having pitched on Thursday, Erik Miller took the mound in the ninth and walked three men. He allowed a run to score on a Victor Mesa Jr. groundout, and the third walk to Caminero brought the winning run to the plate with two outs.
Miller struck out Ryan Vilade, but the ball got away from Connor Wong and the Rays batter reached safely to extend the game and load the bases. But Miller fought back and drew a game-ending groundout from Chandler Simpson, leaving the Rays 0 for 13 with runners in scoring position and 12 men left on base in spite of the nine walks issued by the Red Sox pitching staff.
While Miller has now walked seven batters over his last 3 1/3 innings, Tracy said he felt the left-hander looked much better on Friday despite all of the traffic.
“I thought he was way more competitive,” Tracy said. “Everything was around the zone, stuff was good, he was getting some swing and miss like he usually does so I take a lot of good out of that outing.”
The win marked Boston’s first at Tropicana Field this season, and the club hopes plenty more will follow in the days and weeks to come. The Rays have long been in the driver’s seat for the AL East title, and barring a complete collapse over the final week Tampa Bay should soon lock down the American League’s top seed and a bye to the divisional round.
That means if the Red Sox (84-70) can get past the Yankees in the AL Wild Card Series, they’d be headed right back to St. Petersburg to face the Rays in a rematch of the 2021 ALDS.
But first, the Red Sox hope to pop some bottles in the Tropicana Field visitor’s clubhouse before they fly back to Boston. First pitch on Saturday is scheduled for 4:10 p.m.

item.content:encoded:
The Boston Red Sox are set to begin a three-game series against the Tampa Bay Rays at Tropicana Field at 7:10 p.m. EDT on Friday.
Before Friday’s game, the Red Sox announced a notable lineup decision involving outfielder Jarren Duran.
Boston Red Sox Announce Jarren Duran Decision Before Rays Series
Duran is out of the Red Sox’s lineup for Friday’s game. He started in center field in Thursday’s 5-4 win over the Texas Rangers at Globe Life Field in Arlington, Texas.
The Rays are starting left-hander Ian Seymour on the mound, which is likely why manager Chad Tracy elected to sit Duran, a left-handed hitter.
Here is the Red Sox’s full lineup for Friday:
- Roman Anthony LF
- Nick Sogard 1B
- Jahmai Jones DH
- Wilyer Abreu RF
- Trevor Story SS
- Caleb Durbin 3B
- Isiah Kiner-Falefa 2B
- Nate Eaton CF
- Connor Wong C
Starting Pitcher: LHP Ranger Suarez (7-4, 3.33 ERA, 130 K)
Here is the Rays’ lineup:
- Yainer Diaz DH
- Jonathan Aranda 1B
- Junior Caminero 3B
- Ryan Vilade 2B
- Chandler Simpson LF
- Jonny DeLuca CF
- Nick Fortes C
- Victor Mesa Jr. RF
- Taylor Walls SS
Starting Pitcher: LHP Ian Seymour (9-6, 4.27 ERA, 150 K)
Looking at Jarren Duran
Duran has had a rough season, posting just 0.2 bWAR and a .203/.259/.359 slash line with 20 home runs and 69 RBI over 143 games.
Just two seasons ago, Duran posted 9.0 bWAR and an .834 OPS with 21 home runs and 75 RBI. He had a solid 2025 season as well, posting 4.9 bWAR and a 114 OPS+.
Duran has especially struggled this month, hitting just .159/.213/.250 in 44 at-bats.
On the bright side, Duran has been a spectacular defender for Boston this year, posting +5 Outs Above Average.
Boston Red Sox Right Now
Before beating the Rangers on Thursday, the Red Sox lost the first two games of the series against Texas. Boston is 5-5 in its last 10 games.
At this point in the season, Boston seems locked in to the second AL Wild Card spot unless something crazy happens. If the standings hold up, the Red Sox will play the New York Yankees in the Wild Card round at Yankee Stadium.

Romy Gonzalez seemed like a staple of the Boston Red Sox's offensive attack plan just a year ago. Now, with the playoffs looming, it's become difficult to see where he fits into the picture.
Having been demoted to Triple-A on Aug. 4, Gonzalez has been patiently waiting his turn. The Red Sox are used to having at least one right-handed bat on the roster who primarily gets his looks against left-handed pitchers, but Jahmai Jones has usurped that role from Gonzalez at least temporarily.
With 14 position players on the current active roster and likely 14 joining the Red Sox for the American League Wild Card Series in two weeks, there's an interesting conversation to have about Gonzalez now that the 30-year-old is having a hot month of September in Triple-A. Where will that conversation lead?
Is Gonzalez a legitimate threat to crack playoff roster?
Gonzalez batted near the top of the order for the Red Sox down the stretch last year whenever there was a lefty on the mound. But he also turned out to be battling a shoulder injury that necessitated surgery at the beginning of spring training and delayed his return to the majors until the end of June.
When he did make his season debut, Gonzalez recently admitted that he rushed his rehab, which might reasonably have thrown his swing out of whack against major league quality pitching. He went 12-for-65 with only one home run and a .572 OPS in his 19 major league games before his demotion.
“Where the team was at and all the injuries we had, it was my plan to kind of rush back and be up there,” Gonzalez said, via Christopher Smith of MassLive. “Obviously, hindsight’s 20/20.”
Now, with the Triple-A season coming to an end this weekend, Gonzalez has to know he might not make it back to the majors at all. But he's got the right attitude about the entire situation, seemingly.
“I’m ready whenever my name’s called,” Gonzalez said, per Smith.
If the Red Sox were going to put Gonzalez on the playoff roster, he'd likely have to displace either Connor Wong or Mickey Gasper. Nate Eaton, the current odd man out, should be replaced by Ceddanne Rafaela by the end of the week.

item.content:encoded:
We've reached the "wake me up for the playoffs" portion of the Boston Red Sox season.
The Red Sox have 12 games remaining on their 2026 regular-season schedule. As of Monday, they sit comfortably in the second American League Wild Card spot with a six-game lead. They're 4.5 games behind the New York Yankees in the Wild Card standings, so barring a shocking development, they'll visit the New York Yankees in the Wild Card Series for the second consecutive year.
Which 26 players will the Red Sox bring with them to the Bronx? Who's on the chopping block? Here's our 26-man playoff roster projection with 15 days until Game 1:
MORE RED SOX
Catcher (2): Adley Rutschman, Connor Wong
Cuts: None
The Red Sox could theoretically cut Wong since he'd barely see the field with Rutschman healthy. If Rutschman went down in that scenario, Mickey Gasper could go behind the plate... but that wouldn't be pretty.
Here's the problem with that approach: If Rutschman gets hurt and the Red Sox add a replacement catcher mid-series, Rutschman would be ineligible for the next playoff round. So if he got hurt in the Wild Card Series, he'd be ineligible for the ALDS and eligible to return in the ALCS.
Putting Wong on the playoff roster ensures that if Rutschman goes down, they won't need to add a mid-series replacement with Wong and Gasper already on board. And while Wong isn't exactly Pudge Rodriguez defensively, he's better than Gasper behind the dish.
Infield (7): Willson Contreras, Trevor Story, Caleb Durbin, Isiah Kiner-Falefa, Nick Sogard, Mickey Gasper, Andruw Monasterio
Cuts: Curtis Mead (IL), Anthony Seigler (IL)
Even with Wong on the roster, Gasper's incredible offensive upside shown in August earns him a roster spot as a bench bat. Monasterio is on the bubble, but recent injuries may have cleared his path to a bench role.
It doesn't look like Mead (wrist) will be healthy in time for the start of the postseason.
Outfield (5): Jarren Duran, Wilyer Abreu, Ceddanne Rafaela, Roman Anthony, Jahmai Jones
Cuts: Eli White (IL), Masataka Yoshida (IL), Nate Eaton
The big question mark here is White's health, as the speedster was recently placed on the 10-day injured list with a foot ligament injury. He'll play a key bench role if healthy, but if he isn't, Jones or Eaton are the top candidates for that fifth outfield spot. We're leaning Jones because of his ability to mash left-handers.
Yoshida (hamstring) probably isn't coming back this year.
Starting rotation (3): Sonny Gray, Payton Tolle, Ranger Suarez
Cuts: Patrick Sandoval
Sandoval just hasn't been reliable, so he draws the short straw. Jake Bennett and the returning Garrett Crochet move to the bullpen -- assuming Crochet is healthy enough to give one or two quality innings in relief.
Bullpen (9): Garrett Crochet, Jake Bennett, Brayan Bello, Greg Weissert, Wyatt Olds, Erik Miller, Tyron Guerrero, Garrett Whitlock, Aroldis Chapman
Cuts: Justin Slaten (IL), Tanner Houck (IL), Johan Oviedo (IL), Alec Gamboa, Jovani Moran, Raymond Burgos
If Slaten's elbow is healthy, he's in, but it doesn't currently look like it will be since he was recently shut down from throwing.
Crochet is trending toward being ready just in time for October. So is Houck, but he hasn't pitched in a big-league game since May 2025, and he hasn't looked sharp in his rehab outings. While his upside is intriguing, we'd leave him off the initial playoff roster.
Brayan Bello makes the cut as a bulk arm after excelling in that role throughout the second half.
